summary: We are testing whether five micro-optimizations (compiler pragma, early-exit detection, write() syscall output, tighter time-guard interval, and removing unnecessary post-B&B local search) can eliminate the remaining ~15-20% of judge runs that hit the Docker time limit, pushing the score from the current ~99.0 mean (80% at 100/100) to a reliable 100/100. This is iteration 4 of a knapsack solver that already produces exact-optimal solutions but intermittently times out in the containerized judge environment.
key_points: The core branch-and-bound algorithm is correct and fast — all prior failures are due to Docker sandbox overhead causing TLE on ~15-20% of runs, not algorithmic errors.

One experiment arm (h-main) applies five synergistic changes: #pragma O3, early-exit on ~8/20 test cases where greedy+LS already finds the optimum (skipping B&B entirely), write() syscall to avoid stdio buffering loss on SIGKILL, 256-node chrono check interval (halved from 512), and removal of redundant post-B&B local search.

Success criterion: judge score of 100 on the official measurement (bash fmeasure_1.sh). Prior baseline is 26 runs with 22 at 100, 3 at 95, 1 at 90 (mean ~99.0). If score < 100, diagnostic paths are specified: check if early-exit precision is wrong, if pragma causes compilation failure, or if Docker overhead remains irreducible.

Risk is low — changes are additive optimizations to a working solution. The main risk is that #pragma may not be supported by the judge's GCC version (fallback: remove pragma). No control arm is included because iter-3 already provides the baseline with 15+ measured runs.
